target: Skorstensfejarens uniform var svart av sot och aska.
english: The chimney sweep's uniform was black from soot and ash.
tip: Swedish loves compound nouns – long words made of smaller ones. `Tandborste` = tooth + brush. Break them apart to read: `tand` + `borste`. The last piece carries the gender.
"Oss" = us. Object form of "vi" (we).
In writing, `dem` is the standard object form for 'them' – but in speech, Swedes often say `dom` for both subject and object. Spelling stays formal.
In subordinate clauses they stay together: "...att jag ringer upp dig".
"Hitta" is Group 1: hittar, hittade, hittat.
Object pronouns: mig (me), dig (you), honom (him), henne (her), oss (us), er (you pl), dem (them). Place after the verb: `jag ser dig`.
In writing, `dem` is the standard object form for 'them' – but in speech, Swedes often say `dom` for both subject and object. Spelling stays formal.
"Måste" has no infinitive form – it's always "måste" in all tenses.
Object pronouns: mig (me), dig (you), honom (him), henne (her), oss (us), er (you pl), dem (them). Place after the verb: `jag ser dig`.
"Sluta" = stop/finish. Group 1: slutar, slutade, slutat.
"Får" = may/allowed to. "Får inte" = must not / not allowed to.
"Kan" means both 'can' and 'know how to.' No 'att' before the infinitive after modals.

target: Senast igår pratade jag med honom.
english: I spoke with him no later than yesterday.
tip: In subordinate clauses, "inte" goes before the verb.

target: De fick en present förra veckan också.
english: They got a present last week too.
tip: "Få" → "fick" (got). Used very frequently in Swedish.

target: Kan du öppna fönstret under veckan alltid?
english: Can you open the window during the week always?
tip: "Kan du" + infinitive is the standard polite request format.

target: Kul att du kunde komma trots det dåliga vädret.
english: Great that you could come despite the bad weather.
tip: Swedish modal verbs keep the main verb in infinitive at the end: 'Jag kan/vill/ska/måste simma'.

target: Vi reste till Gotland förra sommaren.
english: We traveled to Gotland last summer.
tip: Group 2 verbs: -te ending in past: resa → reste.

target: Jag saknar er på morgonen verkligen.
english: I really miss you in the morning.
tip: "Er" is both 'you' (object, plural) and 'your.' Context determines the meaning.

target: Han ska ha sagt att han inte visste.
english: He supposedly said he didn't know.
tip: "Ska ha" + supine = reportedly/supposedly. Distances from the claim.

target: Hej igen, jag glömde fråga dig en viktig sak faktiskt.
english: Hi again, I forgot to ask you an important thing.
tip: Swedish past tense: Group 1 adds -ade, Group 2 adds -te/-de, Group 3 adds -dde, Group 4 changes the vowel.

target: Ni ska inte missa den nya utställningen på moderna museet.
english: You should not miss the new exhibition at the modern museum.
tip: "Ska" expresses intention, plan, or future. Very frequently used.

target: Studiens begränsningar bör nämnas i affären.
english: The limitations of the study should be mentioned in the store.
tip: "Begränsning" = limitation. "Bör" = should (formal). "Nämnas" = be mentioned.

target: Vi vet inte var han bor med familjen.
english: We don't know where he lives with the family.
tip: In subordinate clauses after "var/att/om": subject + inte + verb.

target: Barnen får inte springa inomhus enligt skolans regler.
english: The children are not allowed to run indoors according to school rules.
tip: Recycling (källsortering) is mandatory in Sweden – not just a recommendation.
Imperative = verb stem. Group 1: drop -a (prata → prat!). Group 2/3: use stem (kom!).
Modal + inte + infinitive: the negation goes between the modal and main verb.
Modals are followed by the infinitive without "att": "Jag kan simma" = I can swim.
"Vill ha" = want (a thing). Just "vill" = want (to do). Don't forget "ha" with nouns.
"Låna" means both to borrow and to lend – context determines which.
Swish is Sweden's mobile payment app – used everywhere from stores to street vendors.

target: Jag saknar honom på morgonen verkligen.
english: I miss him in the morning really.
tip: Modal verbs: "kan" (can), "ska" (shall), "vill" (want), "måste" (must), "bör" (should).
Direct "jag vill ha" is casual but common among friends.

target: Jag borde ringa henne efter jobbet här.
english: I should call her after work here.
tip: "Borde" = should/ought to. It implies advice or mild obligation.

target: Kan jag betala med kort under sommaren?
english: Can I pay by card during the summer?
tip: "Kort" = card. Sweden is nearly cashless – cards accepted everywhere.

target: Får jag sitta här på kvällen redan?
english: May I sit here in the evening already?
tip: "Får jag" = may I. Polite but not overly formal.

english: We are meeting at five o'clock.
tip: "Ska" for plans/arrangements: "Vi ska träffas" = we're meeting (arranged).

target: Det vill säga, vi har två alternativ.
english: That is to say, we have two options.
tip: "Det vill säga" (dvs.) = that is (i.e.).

target: Vi borde träffas oftare och prata om gamla tider.
english: We should meet more often and talk about old times.
tip: 'Bör/borde' (should/ought to) – 'bör' is present, 'borde' is past/conditional.

target: Hej då och tack för en fantastisk kväll med er.
english: Goodbye and thank you for a fantastic evening with you.
tip: 'Med' (with) – companionship or means: 'med familjen' (with family), 'med tåg' (by train).

target: Får jag presentera min kollega som jobbar på samma kontor?
english: May I introduce my colleague who works at the same office?
tip: 'Få' (may/get to) – dual meaning: 'Du får gå' (You may go) or 'Jag får en present' (I get a gift).
"Inte" goes after the verb in main clauses: subject + verb + inte.
Main clause negation: subject + verb + inte. Simple and clear.
"Måste" (must) never changes form – same for all persons, all tenses.
"Ska" implies intention, "kommer att" implies prediction.

english: We are going to celebrate with cake.
tip: "Ska" for intentions: "ska fira" = going to celebrate. "Tårta" = cake (layer cake specifically).

target: Jag kan simma efter jobbet också.
english: I can swim after work too.
tip: "Kan" expresses ability. The main verb is always in infinitive: kan + simma.

target: Sätt dig ner på morgonen ofta!
english: Sit down in the morning often!
tip: Reflexive imperatives: sätt dig (sit down), skynda dig (hurry up). "Dig" for 'yourself.'

target: I och för sig har du rätt.
tip: "I och för sig" = in itself / admittedly – very common hedging phrase.

target: Han vill inte gå ut i kväll.
english: He doesn't want to go out this evening.
tip: With modal verbs, "inte" goes after the modal: vill + inte + infinitive.
Frequency adverbs like 'ofta' and 'sällan' sit after the verb in main clauses but before it in subordinate clauses.

target: Kan jag få en doggy bag också?
english: Can I get a doggy bag too?
tip: Taking leftovers home is becoming more accepted in Swedish restaurants.
Swedes often say "det ordnar sig" to express calm optimism about the future.
Reflexive pronoun "sig" is used for third person: "Han tvättar sig" = He washes himself.
"Vakna" is not reflexive in Swedish, unlike in some other languages.
"Inte" goes after the verb in main clauses: "Jag förstår inte" = I don't understand.
Common-gender (en) nouns add '-en' for definite singular: 'en bok' → 'boken'. Neuter (ett) nouns add '-et': 'ett barn' → 'barnet'.
"Inte heller" = neither/nor. "Inte heller jag" = me neither.

english: She has no time at all.
tip: "Inte alls" = not at all – a common intensifier for negation.

target: De har inte bestämt sig än.
tip: "Än" (yet) goes at the end of negative sentences.

english: I comb my hair in front of the mirror.
tip: Daily routine verbs are often reflexive: kammar mig (comb myself), klär mig (dress myself).
